C.S. Lewis's religious writing is weirdly mixed because he combined a positive trait with two negative ones: 

1. He was capable of great psychological insight.

2. He was very poor at logic and reasoning. 

3. He was very good at emulating the superficial verbal forms of reasoning convincingly enough that you can be fooled if you're not very bright or motivated not to examine the argument closely. 

He can observe well but not think well. 

When he was playing to his strength, he could produce "The Screwtape Letters", which even this unregenerate pagan considers to have serious moral depth. When he tried to actually think, he produced laughable disasters like "Lewis's Dioemma".

When I was a teenager, many Christians held Lewis up as the best Christian apologist of his time. What this mainly did was convince me that those many Christians were idiots incapable of spotting even obvious logical flaws. 

Years later I read the Screwtape Letters and developed a bit of respect for Lewis's powers of psychological observation. Without however needing to alter my judgment that he was basically a glib dimwit.

Lewis's trilemma is garbage thinking, and it undermines any objective case for how Christians revere him. 

Any ordinary 12 year old knows that liars don't always lie, and lunatics are not mad about everything. 

Therefore, showing that a man told the truth sometimes about some things doesn't prove him not a liar, and does not prove everything he said to be true. You must examine the credibility of each statement. 

Similarly, showing that a man said a sane thing now and again does not prove he is not mad. You must examine the sanity of each statement. 

Something else that every 12 year old knows is that hearsay is not evidence. We are pretty sure Jesus existed. We are not sure at all that he said everything exactly as it was written in the book. This adds a fourth leg to the trilemma... Liar, Lunatic, Lord, or Legend. 

Arthur Conan Doyle wrote, in the mouth of his character, Sherlock Holmes, that when you remove the impossible, what remains, however improbable, must be truth. 

This makes for a good story, and it tempts people to reason this way... by elimination. But reality doesn't work that way. 

You don't know what's impossible. And if you do, and you eliminate it, you're left with more than one possibility. 

No, there are no short cuts. No neat little essay you can write which proves god exists, and makes him appear in a puff of logic. 

You have to do the legwork, and examine the evidence.
